newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Global accounting rules seen facing tough road.
newsitem.headline: Global accounting rules seen facing tough road.

text.p: Divisions within Europe and intransigence on the part of the United States are at the heart of the struggle to achieve standardised international accounting rules, senior officials said on Tuesday.

At a conference on International Accounting Standards, European Union officials noted that while progress has been made on common rules on accounting, differences still remained among national tax authorities.

"The cooperation between the (European) Commission and member states on accounting issues has considerably improved but it remains difficult in Europe to agree on accounting issues," said Karel Van Hulle, a senior European Commission official.

The International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), an independent body of 13 countries, is charged with establishing standards that would be accepted in all countries. Its self-imposed deadline for such a blueprint is March 1998.
The objective is seen as a necessary step in making it easier for international firms to raise capital on world share markets.

Yet given the influential role of the U.S. equity market and the perception that its accounting standards are of a high quality, there is a sense that U.S. regulators are reluctant to embrace quickly a set of standardised rules.
Several participants acknowledged that any common accounting standards were likely to have to bend towards the U.S. model.
"If we want to have an agreement next year then we have to give comfort to FASB (Financial Accounting Standards Board) and the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)," Van Hulle added.
Some said that intransigence on the part of America's powerful SEC was at the root of the problem.
"There are lots of people in the U.S. who want to keep the status quo," said James Cochrane, senior vice president of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).
The NYSE and other American exchanges have brought pressure on the SEC to allow foreign issuers to register their securities for sale in the United States if they comply with international standards.

A milestone event was the effort several years ago by Germany's Daimler-Benz to get its shares listed on the NYSE while complying only with international standards. They eventually had to present their accounts in accordance with U.S. principles to gain admission.
Cochrane said the United States, the Canadian province of Ontario and Japan were the primary stumbling blocks in reaching an accord on harmonised accounting rules.
Still others noted that some international firms were more comfortable with U.S. accounting rules.

"There is an indication that some multinationals still feel that the application of U.S. GAAP or other national standards fulfil their needs more completely," said Jens Roder, former president of the European Federation of Auditors (FEE).
